questions.text: What is the voting system used to elect MPs to the House of Commons, where the candidate with the most votes in each constituency wins? Give its name.
questions.solution: General elections use First Past the Post: the candidate with the most votes in each constituency wins
questions.hint: Its name comes from horse racing

questions.text: Which part of the UK Parliament is made up of elected MPs?

feedback: Members of the House of Lords are not elected by the public
The Supreme Court is the top court, not part of Parliament
The Cabinet is a group of senior ministers in the government

questions.solution: MPs are elected to the House of Commons at general elections
questions.hint: Think about which House the public votes for

questions.text: What is the term for an area of the UK that elects one MP? Give the term.
questions.solution: The UK is divided into constituencies, each electing one MP
questions.hint: Each MP represents the people who live in one of these

questions.text: Who is the head of state in the UK?

feedback: The Prime Minister is head of the government, not head of state

questions.solution: The UK is a constitutional monarchy: the monarch is head of state, while the Prime Minister leads the government
questions.hint: The UK is a constitutional monarchy

questions.text: What do we call a vote in which all citizens can vote directly on a single issue, such as the 2016 vote on EU membership? Give the term.
questions.solution: A referendum lets voters decide directly on one question
questions.hint: Scotland held one on independence in 2014

questions.text: Who chairs debates in the House of Commons and keeps order?
questions.solution: The Speaker chairs debates in the Commons and must stay politically neutral
questions.hint: This MP gives up party politics to run debates fairly

questions.text: Which statement correctly describes the executive and the legislature in the UK?

options: The executive makes laws; the legislature runs the courts
They are two names for the same thing
The executive is the judges; the legislature is the police
The executive runs the country; the legislature makes laws

questions.solution: The executive (the government) runs the country; the legislature (Parliament) makes laws
questions.hint: Legislation means law-making

questions.text: Which part of the UK has its own devolved Parliament at Holyrood?

feedback: Wales has the Senedd in Cardiff
Northern Ireland has the Assembly at Stormont
England does not have its own devolved parliament

questions.solution: The Scottish Parliament sits at Holyrood in Edinburgh
questions.hint: Holyrood is in Edinburgh

questions.text: What is a manifesto?

options: A list of all voters in an area
A document setting out what a party promises to do if elected
feedback: The list of voters is the electoral register

questions.solution: Before an election each party publishes a manifesto of its policies
questions.hint: Parties publish one before a general election

questions.text: What is the group of senior ministers, chosen by the Prime Minister, who make key government decisions called? Give the term.

feedback.Shadow Cabinet: The Shadow Cabinet is formed by the Official Opposition, not the government

questions.solution: The Cabinet is made up of senior ministers such as the Chancellor and the Home Secretary
questions.hint: Its members include the Chancellor of the Exchequer and the Foreign Secretary

questions.text: What is the final stage of a bill called, when the monarch formally agrees to it so it becomes an Act? Give the term.
questions.solution: After both Houses pass a bill, it receives Royal Assent and becomes an Act of Parliament
questions.hint: No monarch has refused it since 1708

questions.text: What does it mean to say the UK constitution is 'uncodified'?

options: The UK has no constitution at all
The constitution can never be changed
The constitution is not written down in one single document
The constitution was written by the EU

questions.solution: The UK constitution is found in many sources, such as Acts of Parliament, court judgements and conventions
questions.hint: Compare it with the USA, which has one written constitution

questions.text: In one constituency, Ali gets 18,000 votes, Beth gets 15,000 and Cal gets 12,000. Under First Past the Post, what is the result?

options: There is a second round, as nobody has over half the votes
feedback: First Past the Post has no second round; the most votes is enough

questions.solution: Under First Past the Post the candidate with the most votes wins, even without a majority (Ali has 40%)
questions.hint: Under this system you do not need more than half the votes

questions.text: The Scottish Parliament passes a law about schools in Scotland. What does this show?

options: Devolution: some powers have been given to Scotland
The House of Lords controls Scotland
feedback: Education is devolved, not reserved

questions.solution: Education is a devolved power, so the Scottish Parliament makes its own laws on it
questions.hint: Think about which powers were transferred to Scotland in 1999

questions.text: A party wins more than half of the seats in the House of Commons. What is the result usually called?

feedback: A coalition is needed when no party has a majority
A hung parliament means no party has a majority

questions.solution: With more than half the seats, a party can form a majority government on its own
questions.hint: More than half is a majority

questions.text: After a general election, no party has more than half of the seats in the House of Commons. What is this situation called?
questions.solution: A hung parliament can lead to a coalition or a minority government
questions.hint: No single party can win votes in the Commons on its own

questions.text: Two or more parties agree to govern together because no single party has a majority. What is this called? Give the term.
questions.solution: A coalition government is formed by two or more parties working together
questions.hint: This happened in the UK in 2010

questions.text: Which court became the UK's highest court of appeal in 2009? Give its name.

accept: Supreme Court of the United Kingdom

questions.solution: The Supreme Court replaced the law lords in the House of Lords as the top appeal court in 2009
questions.hint: It took over this role from the House of Lords

questions.text: Which stage of a bill in the House of Commons comes straight after the second reading?
questions.solution: First reading, second reading, committee stage, report stage, third reading, then the other House and Royal Assent
questions.hint: Write out the stages in order before you choose

questions.text: In one election, Party X won 35% of the votes and 50% of the seats, while Party Y won 20% of the votes and 2% of the seats. What does this show about First Past the Post?

options: Seats are not always in proportion to votes
Seats are always in proportion to votes
Party X won a majority of the votes

questions.solution: Party X got far more seats than its share of votes, and Party Y far fewer, so the result was not proportional
questions.hint: Compare each party's share of votes with its share of seats

questions.text: The House of Lords asks the House of Commons to change part of a bill. Which role is it carrying out?
questions.solution: A key role of the House of Lords is to check and suggest changes to bills
questions.hint: Think about what the Lords do with bills sent from the Commons

questions.text: Which of these is a reserved matter, still decided by the UK Parliament rather than the Scottish Parliament?

feedback: Education is devolved
Health is devolved
Policing is devolved

questions.solution: Defence and foreign affairs are reserved to Westminster; health, education and policing are devolved
questions.hint: Think about which powers affect the whole UK's relations with other countries

questions.text: What term describes the principle that Parliament can make or unmake any law and no other body can override it? Give the term.
questions.solution: Parliamentary sovereignty means Parliament is the highest law-making body in the UK
questions.hint: Sovereign means having supreme power

questions.text: Describe two ways MPs can hold the government to account.

rubric.model_answer: MPs can question ministers in Parliament, for example at Prime Minister's Questions each week, where the Prime Minister must answer questions in public. MPs also sit on select committees, which investigate the work of government departments, question ministers and officials, and publish reports. MPs can also debate bills and vote against the government.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: identifies one way (e.g. Prime Minister's Questions)
1 mark: explains how it holds the government to account
1 mark: identifies a second way (e.g. select committees, debates, votes)
1 mark: explains how it holds the government to account

questions.solution: Questions, select committees, debates and votes all let MPs check the government
questions.hint: Think about what happens in the Commons each week and what committees do

questions.text: Which statement about First Past the Post is accurate?

options: This system always gives each party seats in exact proportion to its votes
This system is used to elect the Northern Ireland Assembly
This system requires voters to rank all the candidates
This system usually produces a clear winner but can give parties seats out of proportion to their votes
feedback: The Northern Ireland Assembly uses the Single Transferable Vote
Ranking candidates is used in preferential systems such as STV

questions.solution: First Past the Post is simple and often gives a clear result, but it is not proportional
questions.hint: Think about strong government versus fairness to smaller parties

questions.text: Which statement about the House of Lords is accurate?

options: Members of the Lords are not elected by the public
The Lords can permanently block any bill passed by the Commons
Members of the Lords are elected every five years
The Lords chooses the Prime Minister
feedback: The Parliament Acts mean the Lords can usually only delay bills, not block them for ever

questions.solution: No members of the House of Lords are elected by the public; most are appointed for life
questions.hint: Think about how people become members of the Lords

questions.text: Which statement about the separation of powers in the UK is accurate?

options: The judiciary is independent of the government
The Prime Minister is head of the judiciary
The executive and legislature never overlap
feedback: They overlap: ministers are members of Parliament

questions.solution: UK judges are independent; but the executive and legislature overlap, because ministers sit in Parliament
questions.hint: Think about whether government ministers are also MPs or peers

questions.text: Which is an argument FOR keeping First Past the Post?

options: It always gives seats in proportion to votes
It lets smaller parties win many seats
It links each MP to a single local constituency
It means every vote counts equally

questions.solution: Supporters say First Past the Post keeps a clear link between each MP and their local area
questions.hint: Look for a real strength of the system

questions.text: Which statement about UK general elections is accurate?

options: Only MPs can vote in them
They elect the House of Lords
One must be held at least every five years

questions.solution: By law a general election must be held at least every five years
questions.hint: Think about the longest a Parliament can last

questions.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of the First Past the Post voting system.

rubric.model_answer: One advantage is that it usually produces a clear winner with a majority, so the government can carry out its manifesto without depending on other parties. It is also simple and keeps a strong link between each MP and their constituency. One disadvantage is that the number of seats a party wins is often not in proportion to its share of votes, so smaller parties with support spread across the country win few seats and many votes are 'wasted'.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: identifies an advantage (e.g. strong, stable government)
1 mark: explains it
1 mark: identifies a disadvantage (e.g. not proportional)
1 mark: explains it

questions.solution: It gives strong government and local links, but results are not proportional
questions.hint: Think about stable government and fairness to smaller parties

questions.text: Which Act of 1998 made the European Convention on Human Rights part of UK law? Give its name.
questions.solution: The Human Rights Act 1998 lets people use their Convention rights in UK courts
questions.hint: It came into force in 2000

questions.text: How many people sit on a jury in a criminal trial in England and Wales?

feedback: Three is a common number for a bench of magistrates, not a jury

questions.solution: A jury in England and Wales has 12 members, chosen at random
questions.hint: Think of a dozen

questions.text: Which court deals with most less serious criminal cases in England and Wales?

options: The European Court of Human Rights
feedback: The Crown Court deals with serious cases, such as murder

questions.solution: Most criminal cases are dealt with completely in the magistrates' court
questions.hint: Its cases are often heard by volunteers who are not lawyers

questions.text: In a criminal trial, what is the person accused of the crime called? Give the term.
questions.solution: The defendant is the person accused of the crime
questions.hint: This person sits in the dock

questions.text: Which organisation decides whether to prosecute most criminal cases in England and Wales?
questions.solution: The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) decides whether a case should go to court and presents it for the prosecution
questions.hint: Its name tells you it brings prosecutions

questions.text: In which year was the Universal Declaration of Human Rights adopted by the United Nations? Give the year.
questions.solution: The UN adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in December 1948
questions.hint: It was three years after the UN was founded in 1945

questions.text: What is the standard of proof in a criminal case?

options: By a majority vote of MPs
feedback: The balance of probabilities is the standard in civil cases

questions.solution: In a criminal case the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt
questions.hint: The jury must be sure the defendant is guilty

questions.text: Which of these is an example of a civil law case?

options: A dispute between a tenant and a landlord over a deposit
feedback: Burglary is a crime, so it is criminal law
Murder is a crime, so it is criminal law
Dangerous driving is a crime, so it is criminal law

questions.solution: Civil law deals with disputes between people or organisations, such as landlord and tenant cases
questions.hint: Civil cases are disputes, not crimes

questions.text: Which court hears serious criminal cases, such as murder, with a judge and jury?

feedback: The county court deals with civil cases

questions.solution: Serious criminal cases are tried in the Crown Court before a judge and jury
questions.hint: Its name includes a word linked to the monarch

questions.text: In a civil case, what is the person who brings the claim called? Give the term.
questions.solution: The claimant brings a civil case against the defendant
questions.hint: This person makes a claim against someone else

questions.text: What is the age of criminal responsibility in England and Wales? Give the age as a number.
questions.solution: In England and Wales children can be charged with a crime from the age of 10
questions.hint: It is lower than in Scotland, where it is 12

questions.text: Which court deals with most criminal cases involving young people aged 10 to 17?
questions.solution: Youth courts are less formal, with no jury, and the public cannot attend
questions.hint: Its name tells you who it is for

questions.text: Sam, aged 30, is charged with shoplifting a £20 item. In which court will his case start?

feedback: The youth court is for people aged 10 to 17

questions.solution: Every adult criminal case starts in the magistrates' court, and minor cases like this usually finish there
questions.hint: All adult criminal cases start in the same kind of court

questions.text: Priya's employer dismisses her and she believes it was unfair. Where would her claim usually be heard?
questions.solution: Claims about unfair dismissal are heard by an employment tribunal
questions.hint: This is a dispute about work, not a crime

questions.text: A newspaper publishes false claims that damage a person's reputation. Which type of law would that person use to sue?
questions.solution: Defamation is a civil wrong, so the person could sue for damages in a civil court
questions.hint: Suing someone for damages is a civil matter

questions.text: People hold a peaceful march about climate change. Which human right are they using?

options: The right to a fair trial

questions.solution: Freedom of assembly protects the right to meet and protest peacefully
questions.hint: Assembly means people gathering together

questions.text: Which United Nations convention of 1989 sets out the rights of everyone under 18? Give its name.

accept: UN Convention on the Rights of the Child
Convention on the Rights of the Child
United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child

questions.solution: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) lists the rights of everyone under 18
questions.hint: Its name says exactly who it protects

questions.text: What word describes a court clearing a defendant of a criminal charge? Give the term.
questions.solution: An acquittal means the defendant is found not guilty and is free to go
questions.hint: It is the opposite of a conviction

questions.text: Jo, aged 15, is charged with a crime. Which statement about her trial is accurate?

options: She will be tried by a jury at the Supreme Court
Her parents will be tried instead of her
It will usually take place in a youth court, without a jury

questions.solution: Most cases for 10 to 17 year olds go to the youth court, with no jury, and the press cannot usually name the young person
questions.hint: Think about which court deals with young people

questions.text: Which of these is a right protected by the Human Rights Act 1998?

options: The right to a fair trial
The right to free university education

questions.solution: The right to a fair trial (Article 6) is one of the Convention rights in the Human Rights Act
questions.hint: Think about rights linked to courts and justice

questions.text: A magazine wants to publish photos of a celebrity's private wedding without permission. Which pair of rights is in conflict?

options: The right to life and the right to education
Freedom of expression and the right to privacy
The right to a fair trial and freedom of religion
The right to marry and freedom of assembly

questions.solution: The magazine's freedom of expression clashes with the couple's right to respect for private life
questions.hint: One right belongs to the magazine and one to the couple

questions.text: In one year a youth court dealt with 400 cases: 240 ended in a referral order, 100 in a fine and 60 in other sentences. What percentage ended in a referral order?

feedback: Divide by the total, 400, not by 1,000

questions.hint: Divide the referral orders by the total number of cases

questions.text: In a civil case, the claimant must prove their case to what standard? Give the phrase.
questions.solution: In civil cases the claimant must show their case is more likely than not: the balance of probabilities
questions.hint: The claimant must show their version is more likely than not

questions.text: Describe two differences between criminal law and civil law.

rubric.model_answer: Criminal law deals with offences against society, such as theft, and the case is brought by the state, usually through the Crown Prosecution Service; civil law deals with disputes between people or organisations, such as a landlord and tenant, and the case is brought by the claimant. In criminal cases guilt must be proved beyond reasonable doubt and the result can be a fine or prison; in civil cases the standard is the balance of probabilities and the usual remedy is compensation (damages).
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: identifies one difference (e.g. who brings the case)
1 mark: gives an example or detail
1 mark: identifies a second difference (e.g. standard of proof, outcomes)
1 mark: gives an example or detail

questions.solution: They differ in who brings the case, the standard of proof and the outcomes
questions.hint: Think about who brings the case and what happens at the end

questions.text: Which statement about juries in England and Wales is accurate?

options: Juries are used in most civil cases
Jurors are chosen at random from the electoral register
feedback: The judge decides the sentence; the jury decides guilty or not guilty
Juries are used in very few civil cases

questions.solution: Jurors are picked at random from the electoral register; the jury decides the verdict and the judge decides the sentence
questions.hint: Think about how ordinary people are picked for jury service

questions.text: Which statement about the European Convention on Human Rights is accurate?

options: The Convention was drawn up by the Council of Europe, not the European Union
The UK stopped following the Convention when it left the EU
The Convention only applies to EU citizens
feedback: The Convention dates from 1950

questions.solution: The Convention (1950) belongs to the Council of Europe, so leaving the EU did not take the UK out of it
questions.hint: Remember the Council of Europe and the EU are different organisations

questions.text: Which is an argument for using juries?

options: Ordinary citizens take part in justice, so verdicts reflect public standards
Juries always give reasons for their verdicts
Juries make trials quicker and cheaper
feedback: Jurors are ordinary members of the public
Juries do not give reasons for their verdicts
Jury trials usually take longer and cost more

questions.solution: Juries let ordinary people take part in justice and judge cases by everyday standards
questions.hint: Think about who sits on a jury

questions.text: Which statement about the rule of law is accurate?

options: The Prime Minister is above the law
Laws only apply to people over 18
Everyone, including the government, must obey the law
Judges can ignore Acts of Parliament they dislike

questions.solution: The rule of law means everyone is equal under the law and nobody, not even the government, is above it
questions.hint: Think about whether anyone is above the law

questions.text: Which statement about the youth justice system in England and Wales is accurate?

options: Young offenders must be punished exactly as harshly as adults
The youth justice system only deals with civil cases
The youth justice system applies to everyone under 25
The main aim is to prevent offending by children and young people

questions.solution: The law says the main aim of the youth justice system is to prevent offending by children and young people
questions.hint: Think about what the system tries to stop happening again

questions.text: Explain two reasons why human rights are important in a democracy.

rubric.model_answer: Human rights protect individuals from the misuse of state power: for example, the right to a fair trial means nobody can be punished without a proper hearing. They also let citizens take part in democracy: freedom of expression, freedom of assembly and the right to free elections let people criticise the government, campaign and vote, so those in power can be held to account.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: identifies a reason (e.g. protects people from the state)
1 mark: explains it with a named right
1 mark: identifies a second reason (e.g. allows participation)
1 mark: explains it with a named right

questions.solution: Rights protect people from the state and let them take part in democracy
questions.hint: Think about protection from the government and taking part in politics

questions.text: In which city is the headquarters of the United Nations?

feedback: Geneva hosts important UN offices, but the headquarters is in the USA
Brussels is home to the main EU institutions

questions.solution: The UN headquarters is in New York City
questions.hint: It is in the USA

questions.text: In which year was the United Nations founded? Give the year.
questions.solution: The United Nations was founded in 1945 to keep international peace
questions.hint: It was set up at the end of the Second World War

questions.text: What is the Commonwealth?

options: A military alliance led by the USA
A voluntary association of countries, most of which were once part of the British Empire
feedback: That describes NATO

questions.solution: The Commonwealth is a voluntary group of independent countries, most with historical links to the British Empire
questions.hint: Think about the countries that were once ruled by Britain

questions.text: What is the term for people coming to live in a country from abroad? Give the term.

feedback.emigration: Emigration means leaving your own country to live somewhere else
feedback.emigrant: Emigration means leaving your own country to live somewhere else
feedback.emigrants: Emigration means leaving your own country to live somewhere else

questions.solution: Immigration means people moving into a country to live there
questions.hint: Think of the word for someone who arrives to settle in a new country

questions.text: Which of these is a role of a free press in a democracy?

options: Informing the public and scrutinising people in power

questions.solution: A free press informs citizens and investigates those in power
questions.hint: Think about what newspapers and broadcasters do

questions.text: Which organisation regulates TV and radio broadcasting in the UK? Give its name.
questions.solution: Ofcom regulates TV and radio and deals with complaints about programmes
questions.hint: It also regulates phone and postal services

questions.text: How many permanent members does the UN Security Council have?

feedback: The Security Council has 15 members in total, but only some are permanent

questions.solution: The five permanent members are China, France, Russia, the UK and the USA
questions.hint: Think of the main winning powers of the Second World War

questions.text: Which of these countries is a permanent member of the UN Security Council?
questions.solution: The UK is one of the five permanent members, each with a veto
questions.hint: The five permanent members were the main winning powers of the Second World War

questions.text: What does 'identity' mean in Citizenship?

options: How people see themselves and the groups they feel they belong to

questions.solution: Identity is about how we see ourselves, for example through nationality, religion, culture and family
questions.hint: Think about the answer to the question 'Who am I?'

questions.text: What term describes the freedom of newspapers and broadcasters to report without government control? Give the term.
questions.solution: Press freedom lets journalists report and criticise without government censorship
questions.hint: It is linked to the human right of freedom of expression

questions.text: What word describes a society in which people of many different ethnic, religious and cultural backgrounds live together? Give the term.
questions.solution: The UK is a multicultural, diverse society
questions.hint: Think of a word that means many cultures together

questions.text: Which term describes someone who has had to leave their country because of war or persecution and has been given protection in another country?

feedback: An economic migrant moves mainly for work or a better standard of living

questions.solution: A refugee has fled war or persecution and has been given protection in another country
questions.hint: The word is linked to 'refuge', meaning a place of safety

questions.text: Amira was born in Leeds, her parents grew up in Pakistan, and she supports Leeds United. What does this show about identity?

options: Identity depends only on where your parents were born
People can have several identities at once

questions.solution: Amira can feel British, a Leeds fan and proud of her Pakistani heritage all at once
questions.hint: Count how many groups Amira belongs to

questions.text: A newspaper reveals that a government minister misused public money. Which role of a free press does this show?
questions.solution: Investigative journalism holds people in power to account by revealing wrongdoing
questions.hint: Think about who was being checked

questions.text: Which UN body can authorise military action to keep international peace and security?
questions.solution: The UN Security Council can approve peacekeeping missions, sanctions and military action
questions.hint: It has five permanent members with a veto

questions.text: A family moves from Poland to the UK to find better-paid work. What type of migration is this?

feedback: Forced migration is when people have to leave, for example because of war
Internal migration is moving within the same country

questions.solution: Moving by choice for work is economic migration
questions.hint: Think about the reason the family moved

questions.text: Which international organisation, founded in 1945, has a General Assembly where every member state has one vote? Give its name.
questions.solution: In the United Nations General Assembly every member state has one vote
questions.hint: Its headquarters is in New York

questions.text: What term describes treating someone unfairly because of a characteristic such as race, religion or disability? Give the term.

feedback.prejudice: Prejudice is an unfair opinion or attitude; acting on it is a different word

questions.solution: Discrimination is treating someone unfairly because of who they are; the Equality Act 2010 makes it illegal
questions.hint: The Equality Act 2010 makes this illegal

questions.text: A town has a population of 50,000. Of these, 7,500 people were born outside the UK. What percentage is this?
questions.hint: Divide 7,500 by 50,000, then multiply by 100

questions.text: Which law brought together earlier anti-discrimination laws and lists 'protected characteristics'?

options: The Representation of the People Act 1928
feedback: The Human Rights Act brought European Convention rights into UK law
The 1928 Act gave women the vote on equal terms with men

questions.solution: The Equality Act 2010 protects people from discrimination based on nine protected characteristics
questions.hint: It is named after the idea of treating people fairly

questions.text: Which statement about the Commonwealth is accurate?

options: Member countries must use the pound
Member countries are independent and share values such as democracy
Member countries are governed from London
Only countries in Europe can join

questions.solution: Commonwealth members are independent equals who cooperate on shared values
questions.hint: Think about whether members are ruled by Britain today

questions.text: In 2016 the UK held a referendum on membership of the European Union. What was the result?
questions.solution: About 52% voted to leave and 48% to remain; the UK left the EU in January 2020
questions.hint: The result is often called Brexit

questions.text: Which human right lets journalists criticise the government without being punished? Give the right.
questions.solution: Freedom of expression (Article 10) protects the right to hold and share opinions, though it has some limits
questions.hint: It is Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights

questions.text: Describe two benefits of a diverse society for the UK.

rubric.model_answer: Diversity brings a wider range of skills and ideas: migrants have helped to staff public services such as the NHS and have started many businesses. It also enriches culture, for example through food, music, festivals and languages, and helps people learn about and respect different ways of life.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: identifies one benefit (e.g. economic, skills)
1 mark: supporting example
1 mark: identifies a second benefit (e.g. culture, understanding)
1 mark: supporting example

questions.solution: Diversity can strengthen the economy and enrich culture
questions.hint: Think about work and skills, and about culture

questions.text: Which statement about press freedom in the UK is accurate?

options: The press can publish anything with no legal limits
The government decides what newspapers print each day
Only the BBC is allowed to report news
Press freedom has limits, such as laws against defamation and contempt of court

questions.solution: The press is free from government control but must obey laws such as defamation and contempt of court
questions.hint: Think about what happens if a newspaper prints false claims about someone

questions.text: Which of these is one of the 'fundamental British values' that schools in England must promote?

options: Belonging to the Church of England

questions.solution: The values are democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, and mutual respect and tolerance
questions.hint: Think about values that apply to everyone, whatever their beliefs

questions.text: Which statement about the UK's role in the United Nations is accurate?

options: The UK left the UN when it left the EU
The UK is a permanent member of the Security Council, with a veto
The UK has no vote in the General Assembly
The UK hosts the UN headquarters
feedback: The UN headquarters is in New York

questions.solution: As a permanent member of the Security Council the UK can veto resolutions
questions.hint: Think about the five permanent members

questions.text: Which is a reason some people argue that a free press is vital to democracy?

options: It lets the government control public opinion
It replaces the need for elections
Voters need accurate information to make choices at elections

questions.solution: Democracy needs informed voters, and a free press gives them information about parties and policies
questions.hint: Think about what voters need before an election

questions.text: In a town, people from different backgrounds rarely mix. Which of these actions aims to build community cohesion?

options: Holding a festival where different community groups share their food and music

questions.solution: Shared events help people from different backgrounds meet and build trust
questions.hint: Look for the option that brings people together

questions.text: Explain two ways the UK works with other countries through international organisations.

rubric.model_answer: Through the United Nations the UK, as a permanent member of the Security Council, helps make decisions about peacekeeping and sanctions, and it has provided troops and funding for UN peacekeeping missions. Through NATO it works with allies on collective defence. Through the Commonwealth it cooperates with member countries on trade, education and promoting democracy.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: names an organisation (e.g. the UN)
1 mark: explains the UK's role in it
1 mark: names a second organisation (e.g. NATO, Commonwealth)
1 mark: explains the UK's role in it

questions.solution: The UK works through the UN, NATO and the Commonwealth
questions.hint: Think about peacekeeping, defence and the Commonwealth

questions.text: What do we call a group that tries to influence government decisions on a particular issue without standing for election? Give the term.
questions.solution: Pressure groups, such as Greenpeace and Shelter, campaign to influence decisions
questions.hint: Greenpeace and Shelter are examples

questions.text: What is a petition?

options: A formal request signed by many people asking for action

questions.solution: A petition shows decision-makers how many people support a request
questions.hint: People sign it to show their support

questions.text: What is the term for giving your time without pay to support a charity or your community? Give the term.
questions.solution: Volunteering means giving your time freely, without pay
questions.hint: People who do this are not paid

questions.text: What is a trade union?

options: A company that sells goods abroad
An organisation that represents workers and campaigns for their rights

questions.solution: Trade unions represent workers, for example in negotiations about pay and conditions
questions.hint: Its members are workers

questions.text: Which of these is an example of active citizenship?

options: Volunteering at a local food bank

questions.solution: Active citizens take part in their community, for example by volunteering
questions.hint: Look for the option where someone takes part

questions.text: What is the term for refusing to buy a company's products as a form of protest? Give the term.
questions.solution: A boycott puts economic pressure on a company to change
questions.hint: The word comes from the name of a 19th-century land agent in Ireland

questions.text: Which describes an insider pressure group?

options: A group that only uses illegal protest
A political party that stands in elections
A group the government regularly consults

questions.solution: Insider groups have close links with government and are consulted on policy
questions.hint: Inside means close to decision-makers

questions.text: What is lobbying?

options: Trying to persuade MPs or officials to support a cause

questions.solution: Lobbying means contacting and persuading decision-makers, such as MPs
questions.hint: The word comes from the lobbies of Parliament where MPs can be met

questions.text: What is a strike?

options: When a company closes for a holiday
When workers refuse to work to put pressure on an employer
When a court fines a worker
When MPs vote on a bill

questions.solution: A strike is when workers stop working, usually after a union ballot, to win better pay or conditions
questions.hint: It is a form of action by workers

questions.text: Which organisation registers and regulates charities in England and Wales? Give its name.

accept: Charity Commission for England and Wales

questions.solution: The Charity Commission registers charities and checks they follow the rules
questions.hint: It keeps a public register of every registered charity

questions.text: What is the term for a large public march or gathering to show support for or opposition to a cause? Give the term.
questions.solution: A demonstration is a public gathering or march to show support for or opposition to something
questions.hint: Thousands of people may walk through a city carrying banners

questions.text: What do trade unions do in 'collective bargaining'?

options: Vote in general elections for their members
Negotiate pay and conditions with employers for their members
Set the national minimum wage on their own

questions.solution: Collective bargaining means a union negotiates for all its members together
questions.hint: Collective means as a group

questions.text: Students want their school to install water fountains. Which of these is a democratic way for them to raise it?

options: Refuse to attend lessons for a month
Raise it through the school council

questions.solution: A school council is an elected body where students can raise issues democratically
questions.hint: Think about elected student representatives

questions.text: Residents collect 2,000 signatures asking the council to put in a pedestrian crossing. Which method are they using?
questions.solution: Collecting signatures for a request is a petition
questions.hint: Think about what the signatures are for

questions.text: An environmental group holds protests outside Parliament and gets media coverage, but has no regular contact with government ministers. What type of pressure group is it?
questions.solution: Outsider groups are not consulted by government, so they use protests and the media
questions.hint: Is the group consulted by ministers or not?

questions.text: Which of these is a way that social media can support a campaign?

options: Guaranteeing a law will be changed
Letting people vote in general elections online
Spreading information quickly to large numbers of people

questions.solution: Social media lets campaigns reach many people quickly and cheaply
questions.hint: Think about how fast a post can be shared

questions.text: What is the term for a person elected to represent a local area on a council? Give the term.

feedback.counsellor: A counsellor gives advice and support; an elected council member has a different title

questions.solution: Councillors are elected in local elections to represent a ward on the council
questions.hint: They are elected in local elections

questions.text: What is the term for a planned series of actions, such as petitions, events and posts, to achieve a goal? Give the term.
questions.solution: A campaign is an organised set of actions aimed at a goal
questions.hint: Parties run election ones before voting day

questions.text: A charity raised £12,000: £3,000 from a sponsored run, £6,000 from donations and £3,000 from a bake sale. What fraction came from donations?

feedback: 1/4 is the share from the sponsored run (or from the bake sale)

questions.hint: Divide the donations by the total amount raised

questions.text: Which statement about trade unions in the UK is accurate?

options: They can organise legal strikes after a ballot of their members
They are part of the government
They decide sentences in court cases
They are banned in the UK

questions.solution: UK law requires a ballot of members before a lawful strike
questions.hint: Think about how a union decides whether to strike

questions.text: Which is a reason some people argue pressure groups are good for democracy?

options: They let people's views be heard between elections
They replace the need for MPs

questions.solution: Pressure groups give people a way to take part between elections
questions.hint: Think about what citizens can do between general elections

questions.text: In which year did a law first give some women the right to vote in UK general elections?

feedback: In 1928 women got the vote on equal terms with men
In 1969 the voting age was lowered to 18

questions.solution: The Representation of the People Act 1918 gave the vote to some women over 30
questions.hint: It was passed at the end of the First World War

questions.text: Which campaigners for women's votes, led by Emmeline Pankhurst, used direct action? Give the name of the group's members.

feedback.suffragists: Suffragists campaigned peacefully, mainly through the NUWSS led by Millicent Fawcett
feedback.suffragist: Suffragists campaigned peacefully, mainly through the NUWSS led by Millicent Fawcett

questions.solution: The suffragettes of the WSPU, founded by Emmeline Pankhurst in 1903, used direct action
questions.hint: Their slogan was 'Deeds not words'

questions.text: Describe two ways a young person could campaign for a change in their local area.

rubric.model_answer: They could start a petition, online or on paper, and present it to the local council or their MP to show how many people support the change. They could also contact their local councillor or MP by email or letter, or arrange a meeting, and use social media and the local press to raise awareness. Joining a youth council or organising a peaceful event are other ways.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: identifies one method (e.g. petition)
1 mark: explains how it could bring change
1 mark: identifies a second method (e.g. contacting a councillor, social media)
1 mark: explains how it could bring change

questions.solution: Petitions, contacting representatives and raising awareness are all ways to campaign
questions.hint: Think about who has the power to make the change, and how to reach them

questions.text: Which statement about pressure groups' methods is accurate?

options: Pressure groups must stand candidates in elections
Pressure groups are not allowed to use the media
Some use direct action, such as protests, while others lobby ministers privately

questions.solution: Methods vary: outsider groups often use protests, while insider groups lobby government directly
questions.hint: Think about the difference between insider and outsider groups

questions.text: Why might a campaign group choose peaceful protest rather than breaking the law?

options: To keep public support and avoid arrest

questions.solution: Peaceful, legal protest keeps public sympathy and avoids members being arrested
questions.hint: Think about how the public reacts to different kinds of protest

questions.text: Which is a criticism sometimes made of pressure groups?

options: They let ordinary people be heard
Wealthy groups may have more influence than others
They encourage people to take part

questions.solution: Critics say groups with more money and contacts can have unfair influence
questions.hint: Look for the option that is a weakness, not a strength

questions.text: Which statement about charities is accurate?

options: Charities are run by the Prime Minister
Charities must make a profit for shareholders
Charities are independent of government, though some receive government funding
Charities may not campaign on any issue

questions.solution: Charities are independent, not-for-profit organisations; some get government grants and many campaign
questions.hint: Think about who runs a charity and where its money goes

questions.text: Which statement about volunteering in the UK is accurate?

options: Volunteering is compulsory for all adults
Volunteers give their time freely and are not paid wages

questions.solution: Volunteers choose to give their time without pay
questions.hint: Think about what voluntary means

questions.text: Explain two reasons why active citizenship is important in a democracy.

rubric.model_answer: Active citizens take part beyond voting, for example by campaigning, volunteering or joining pressure groups, so decision-makers hear a wider range of views and can be held to account between elections. Active citizenship also strengthens communities: volunteers support local services and charities, and people working together on local issues builds trust and cohesion.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: identifies a reason (e.g. holding power to account)
1 mark: explains it with an example
1 mark: identifies a second reason (e.g. stronger communities)
1 mark: explains it with an example

questions.solution: Active citizens hold leaders to account and strengthen communities
questions.hint: Think about decision-makers and about local communities
